title: Plafonddienst
excerpt: Plafonddienst (ceiling duty) is lying awake and staring at the ceiling after using stimulants, unable to sleep.
example: After the festival he did hours of plafonddienst before he finally fell asleep.
text: It happens when something keeps you wide awake long after the party is over. Your body is tired, your brain is not. The tip: stop with anything that keeps you up well before you want to sleep. And skip the coffee at midnight too.

title: Plot twist
excerpt: A plot twist is an unexpected turn that changes how you see everything.
example: "I thought he was single. Plot twist: he's had a girlfriend for three years."
text: The term comes from films and books. Now people use it for surprising moments in real life. Often in jokes, stories and captions. Every great party story needs one.

title: Pocketing
excerpt: Pocketing means hiding your partner from your friends, family or social media.
example: "We've been together for six months, but I've never met a single friend of his." That sounds like pocketing.
text: Your partner is in your pocket, out of sight. A bit of privacy is normal. But if someone keeps hiding you, that can be a red flag. The opposite is a hard launch.

title: POV
excerpt: POV stands for point of view. On social media you put yourself in someone else's situation.
example: "POV: your housemate says he's only coming for one beer."
text: POV videos show a situation as if you are in it. The camera plays your eyes. The format is huge on TikTok and Instagram Reels. Usually about relatable or funny moments.

title: Praeses
excerpt: The praeses is the chair of the board of a Dutch student association, dispuut or committee.
example: As praeses she opened the ALV with a short, formal speech.
text: The praeses has the final responsibility and is the face of the board. Their closest colleagues are the ab actis and the assessor. The word is Latin for president. Being praeses is a big deal. It usually comes with a lot of speeches.

title: Pre-drinks
excerpt: Pre-drinks are drinks with friends before going to the bar, club or party.
example: "Pre-drinks at mine at nine, then into town at eleven."
text: Pre-drinks is mostly British. Americans say pregame. The Dutch call it indrinken. You already have a good time together and it saves money at the bar.

title: Prela
excerpt: A prela (pre-relationship) is the stage right before an official relationship. You are exclusive, but not a rela yet.
example: After a few months of dating they secretly started calling it their prela.
text: A prela starts when you keep seeing the same person and you are exclusive. Often a prela grows into a real rela. Dutch students have a word for every step: eventuela, scharrel, kwarrel, prela, rela.

title: Pro tip
excerpt: A pro tip is handy advice, given as if it comes from an expert.
example: "Pro tip: eat a cheese sandwich before the gala. You'll thank me tomorrow."
text: A pro tip can be sincere or a joke. Often it is a small lesson you learned the hard way. It is close to a life hack.

title: Proleet
excerpt: Proleet is a snobby Dutch word for someone with no class. Students sometimes use it for people who never studied.
example: "Don't talk like a proleet," she joked to her brother.
text: It comes from proletarian. Among students it is used for someone who never went to university, a bit like arbeider or burger. It is snobby on purpose. Mostly said as a joke between friends.

title: Promi
excerpt: Promi is short for prominent: a well-known, very active member of a Dutch student association.
example: "She's really promi in the association," he said admiringly.
text: The short version is mostly used when people talk about who is actively involved in the club. Promi's are on every committee and know everyone. You will see them at every borrel.

title: Prominent
excerpt: Prominent describes a member who does lots of committees and is important within a Dutch student association.
example: As a prominent member he was already on his third committee at the same time.
text: A prominent member does a lot of committees and plays a big role in the club. Often called promi for short. It is basically clout, association style.

title: Propedeuse
excerpt: The propedeuse is the certificate that shows you passed all the credits of your first year at a Dutch university.
example: With her propedeuse in the bag she threw a big party with her housemates.
text: The certificate, also called your P, is what you get when you pass all the credits of the first year of your bachelor. For hbo students it can also be a stepping stone to a research university. It means you are safe from a negative BSA.

title: Pub
excerpt: A pub is a bar, especially in the UK and Ireland, where you drink, eat and meet people.
example: "In Dublin we went to the same pub every night. After three days the bartender knew our names."
text: Pub comes from public house. A pub is usually calmer than a club. It is a local spot where you have a pint with friends and sometimes do a quiz. A night visiting lots of pubs is a pub crawl.

title: Pub crawl
excerpt: A pub crawl is a night where a group goes from one bar to the next.
example: "For his birthday we're doing a pub crawl past ten bars. One drink in each."
text: Pub crawl is the British and Irish name. Americans say bar crawl. The Dutch call it a kroegentocht. Lots of associations organise one during the introductieweek.

title: Quaestor / Quaestrix
excerpt: The quaestor (or quaestrix) is the treasurer on the board of a Dutch student association.
example: As quaestor she presented the annual accounts of the association at the ALV.
text: Also called fiscus or thesaurier. This person handles the money: making budgets, keeping the cash and paying the bills for the association, dispuut or student house. Another Latin title, because of course it is.

title: Quarter-life crisis
excerpt: A quarter-life crisis is a time of doubt about your studies, work, relationships or direction, usually in your twenties.
example: "Everyone around me is buying a house or getting married and I don't even know what I want after my master." Classic quarter-life crisis.
text: When your studies end, big choices suddenly show up. Work, money, housing and relationships. Lots of people in their twenties feel pressure and uncertainty. It is the younger version of the midlife crisis. And you are definitely not the only one.

title: Queue
excerpt: A queue is a line of people waiting for something, like at the club or the snack bar.
example: "The queue for the club went all the way to the corner. Luckily we were on the guest list."
text: Queue is mostly British English. Americans say line. The British are famous for queueing very neatly. Cutting the queue there is almost a crime.

title: Rage bait
excerpt: Rage bait is online content made on purpose to make you angry, so you react and the post gets more reach.
example: "That video of someone putting ketchup on pizza? Pure rage bait. Just don't react."
text: The more people react angrily, the more the algorithm shows the post. That is why rage bait works so well. It was Oxford Word of the Year in 2025. It is like clickbait, but it plays on anger instead of curiosity.

title: Ratio
excerpt: A ratio is when a reply to a post gets way more likes than the post itself.
example: "His tweet got a hundred likes. The reply under it got two thousand. He got ratioed."
text: The term got big on X, back when it was Twitter. If you get ratioed, more people agree with the reply than with you. Sometimes people just reply "ratio", hoping it works.

title: Rattentaxi
excerpt: Taking the rattentaxi (rat taxi) means sneaking away from a night out without saying goodbye.
example: Around three he was suddenly gone. He took the rattentaxi again.
text: Just leaving like that is seen as a bit rude. Unless you are too drunk to say a proper goodbye, then everyone understands. Also called a houdini. In English: an Irish goodbye.

title: Reaction video
excerpt: A reaction video is a video where someone films their reaction to another video, song or news.
example: "I'd rather watch that streamer's reaction video than the trailer itself."
text: Reaction videos are popular because you see the original and the personality of the creator. They are huge on YouTube and TikTok. On TikTok you often do it with a duet or stitch.

title: Real
excerpt: You reply real when you totally recognise yourself in something or agree with it.
example: "After one beer I already feel responsible for the whole group." "Real."
text: A simple "real" under a post or in a text means: so relatable. It is close to mood, facts or period. You don't literally mean something is real.

title: Rebound
excerpt: A rebound is someone you start something with soon after a breakup, often to forget your ex.
example: "She's been single for two weeks and already has someone new. Isn't that just a rebound?"
text: Rebound comes from basketball, where it is a ball bouncing back. A rebound relationship is often more about distraction than real feelings. That is why it usually doesn't last long.

title: Receipts
excerpt: Receipts are screenshots, messages or other proof that show what really happened.
example: "He says he never said that? I have the receipts. Here's the screenshot."
text: Receipts come from the slip that proves you bought something. In online drama it is often about who has the receipts. A screenshot ends any discussion.

title: Red flag
excerpt: A red flag is a warning sign. Behaviour that shows someone or something isn't good for you.
example: "He was rude to the waiter and talked about his ex the whole date. Red flag after red flag."
text: A red flag means danger. In dating it is about things like jealousy, lying or wanting control. A small annoyance usually isn't a red flag. The opposite is a green flag.

title: Regelen
excerpt: Regelen (to arrange) is Dutch student slang for kissing or hooking up with someone.
example: "Did you regelen anything last night?" her housemate asked.
text: In normal Dutch regelen means organising something. Among students it covers anything romantic or physical, from just kissing to going further. So if someone says they regelde something at the party, they don't mean the drinks.

title: Regenjas
excerpt: Regenjas (raincoat) is Dutch student slang for a condom.
example: "Don't forget your regenjas," her friend joked before she left.
text: It is one of several student nicknames for the same thing, next to condo and connie. Whatever you call it, bring one.

title: Rela
excerpt: Rela is Dutch slang for a relationship, the stage after the prela.
example: After a year of dating they finally made it an official rela.
text: At this stage you are exclusive, you met each other's parents and you are officially together. Unlike the more casual prela before it. Time for the hard launch on Instagram.

title: Relationship goals
excerpt: You say relationship goals about a relationship others admire and would love to have themselves.
example: "They cook together every Sunday and still laugh at each other's jokes. Relationship goals."
text: You often see it under romantic photos. Keep in mind that social media only shows part of a relationship. It is close to couple goals.

title: Rent free
excerpt: Rent free means something or someone keeps showing up in your thoughts, even though you don't want it to.
example: "That song from the party has been living rent free in my head for three days."
text: The idea is that something lives in your head without paying rent. Songs, jokes, exes or arguments. Embarrassing memories can live rent free in your head for years. As a student in the Netherlands, living anywhere rent free sounds like a dream.

title: Reparadler
excerpt: A reparadler (repair radler) is a radler you drink to ease your hangover.
example: The morning after the borrel he grabbed a reparadler right away.
text: A radler is beer mixed with lemonade. It goes down as easily as soda, so students swear by it the morning after. The proof that it works is thin. It is the lighter version of the herstelbiertje.

title: Reünist
excerpt: A reünist is a former member of a Dutch student association or dispuut.
example: As a reünist she still came back every year for the lustrum trip.
text: Reünisten often stay closely involved with their old association or dispuut, long after graduating. They show up at the dies, the lustrum and sometimes with a big donation. Once a member, always a member.

title: Riet
excerpt: Riet is Dutch student slang for a straw, often used to chug a drink faster.
example: "Does anyone have a riet for this bottle?" he asked at the table.
text: Riet means reed, the plant straws used to be made of. Students use one to do a rietadt or rietbak. That way a drink is gone even faster than the normal way.

title: Rietadt
excerpt: A rietadt is an adtje through a straw, a faster way to finish a drink in one go.
example: For the contest he went for a rietadt instead of a normal chug.
text: For advanced drinkers, a rietadt (also called rietbak) goes faster than a normal adtje. The straw lets air in and the drink flows fast. It is a lot like chugging, with a little help.

title: Rietbak
excerpt: Rietbak is another word for rietadt: chugging a beer through a straw.
example: "Just do a rietbak, then it's done in no time," she said firmly.
text: It is used interchangeably with rietadt and means the same straw trick. Some people also use it for a person who chugs with a straw. Either way, it is fast.

title: RIP
excerpt: RIP stands for rest in peace. Online it is also used as a joke when something goes wrong.
example: "I spilled beer on my laptop. RIP my thesis."
text: Originally you use RIP when someone dies. Online people also use it for small losses or failures. Your broken phone, your missed deadline or your first hangover of the year.

title: Rizz
excerpt: Rizz is charm or flirting talent. Someone with rizz can win someone over with a few words or a look.
example: "He said one sentence to her and she gave him her number right away. That guy seriously has rizz."
text: Rizz comes from charisma. The word blew up through streamer Kai Cenat and TikTok, and was even Oxford Word of the Year in 2023. Trying to flirt is rizzing someone up. Pulling it off without saying a word? That is unspoken rizz.

title: RN
excerpt: RN stands for right now.
example: "I'm on the train RN. Be there in twenty minutes."
text: RN is used a lot in texts and on social media. It can also mean registered nurse. But in normal texts people almost always mean "now".

title: Roasted
excerpt: Getting roasted means being made fun of in a funny, sharp way.
example: "During his birthday speech his housemates roasted him hard."
text: A roast can be friendly or meant to hurt. The difference is in the context and the friendship. Among friends a good roast is often a sign of love.

title: ROFL
excerpt: ROFL stands for rolling on the floor laughing.
example: "He tried to impress her with his dance moves and fell into the pool. ROFL."
text: ROFL is an over-the-top way to say something is really funny. It is old internet slang. These days you see LMAO or "I'm dead" more often.

title: Roommate
excerpt: A roommate is someone you share a room, flat or house with.
example: "My roommate in New York snored so loud I had to sleep with earplugs."
text: In American English a roommate can also be someone you just share a house with. In British English that is a flatmate. In American dorms you really share a room with your roommate. In a Dutch student house you usually get your own room.

title: Safedate
excerpt: A safedate is a date without any romantic intentions, often a friend you take to a datediner or gala.
example: For the datediner she simply asked her best friend to be her safedate.
text: It is clear from the start that nothing romantic will happen. Handy when you don't have a date yet, or just want to be sure of a fun night. Dutch student associations throw a lot of events where you need a date. A safedate solves that.

title: Salty
excerpt: Being salty means you are grumpy or annoyed, often because something didn't go your way.
example: "He lost at Mexico and now he's salty for the rest of the night."
text: Salty is usually about small annoyances or losing a game. Not about real anger. Dutch students settle real arguments with brassen.

title: Savage
excerpt: Savage describes something brutally honest, ruthless or impressively bold.
example: "She told her ex: 'Nice to see you, I'd already forgotten you.' Savage."
text: Savage can be a compliment for a sharp comeback or a bold move. But it can also be about behaviour that is actually mean. The context decides if it is admiration or criticism.

title: Scharrel
excerpt: A scharrel is a casual fling: you hook up regularly and get along, but it isn't a relationship.
example: "Is that your new scharrel?" her housemate asked when she saw him again.
text: You see each other now and then for a relaxed time together, and that is it. No labels, no plans. If it grows into something with feelings, it becomes a kwarrel. In English the closest word is situationship.

title: Screenshotting
excerpt: Screenshotting means taking a picture of what is on your screen, like a text or a post.
example: "I screenshotted his message and put it in the group chat with my friends right away."
text: People use screenshots to save messages, tickets or proof. Some apps let the other person know you took one. In online drama, screenshots are the receipts.

title: Seeing someone
excerpt: Seeing someone means you date someone regularly, without it being an official relationship yet.
example: "Is she single?" "Not really. She's seeing someone, but they don't call it a relationship yet."
text: The phrase is vague on purpose. It can be a few dates or something more serious already. It sits between a talking stage and a real relationship. The Dutch would say scharrel.

title: Semester
excerpt: A semester is half of an academic year.
example: By the end of the first semester she had already passed three exams.
text: At Dutch universities a semester usually has two blocks of courses. Each block ends with exams, papers or projects. Exchange students usually come for one semester. Just long enough to learn what gezellig means.

title: Seminar
excerpt: A seminar is a small class built around discussion and taking part.
example: "In the seminar I had to summarise the article. I had only read the title."
text: A seminar has fewer students than a lecture. There is more talking, asking and discussing. So you do need to prepare. In the Netherlands it is often called a werkgroep or werkcollege.

title: Sending me
excerpt: You say sending me when something makes you laugh really hard.
example: She sent a video of her housemate tripping over a beer crate. "This is sending me."
text: You usually hear it as "this is sending me" or "you're sending me". You are being launched off your chair from laughing. It is close to I'm dead and I'm weak.
